match.reason: The new point teaches graphing y = 1/f(x) in general, including the sec, cosec and cot graphs with asymptotes where f(x) = 0, while the closest bank points cover only y = k/x graphs or the reciprocal trig ratios' values, so neither is the same idea at the right depth.

draft.title: Reciprocal functions
card: The graph of y = 1/f(x) comes from the graph of y = f(x). Each y-value is replaced by its reciprocal, so a point (a, b) becomes (a, 1/b).
Where f(x) = 0, the reciprocal is undefined. So y = 1/f(x) has a vertical asymptote at every x-intercept of f.
Points where f(x) = 1 or f(x) = −1 stay on the graph, because 1/1 = 1 and 1/(−1) = −1. Where f is positive, 1/f is positive. Where f is negative, 1/f is negative.
The reciprocal circular functions are sec x = 1/cos x, cosec x = 1/sin x and cot x = 1/tan x. Example: cos x = 0 at x = π/2, so sec x has a vertical asymptote at x = π/2.
draft.remember: Reciprocal graphs have a vertical asymptote wherever f(x) = 0.

a.q: The graph of y = f(x) crosses the x-axis at x = 3 and x = −2. What does y = 1/f(x) have at these x-values?
a.why: At each x-intercept f(x) = 0, and 1/0 is undefined, so the graph has a vertical asymptote there. It does not have x-intercepts, because 1/f(x) is never 0 when f(x) is a finite number.
a.clue: What happens when you divide 1 by zero?

b.q: Which equation gives the vertical asymptotes of y = cosec x for 0 ≤ x ≤ 2π?
b.why: cosec x = 1/sin x, and sin x = 0 at x = 0, π and 2π. Those are the asymptotes. The values x = π/2 and 3π/2 are where cos x = 0, which gives the asymptotes of sec x, not cosec x.
b.clue: Find where sin x equals zero.
